name: David Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an eight-wheel tipper for a quarry, hauling gravel, sand and crushed stone out to building sites and the asphalt plant. I get loaded by the big shovel, go over the weighbridge, and do maybe six or seven round trips a day. I like the rhythm and the view off the top of the quarry first thing. What wears me out is the dust, and the sites where you wait an hour to tip because nobody's ready.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at the quarry, and how's it going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About fourteen months driving, after two years on the yard loading shovel. I'm still not great at tipping on a slope, and the foreman, Pete, has had words once or twice. I live with my partner Hannah, she's a teaching assistant, and we've got about four months of bills saved, which feels decent for our age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing much changed, which is about what I expected. At the quarry we'd joke that the weighbridge is the only robot we've got. I might share something on the group chat, not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weighbridge already prints my ticket without anyone touching it, and nobody at the quarry lost a job over that. So I keep my job, get better at tipping, and get on with life. Building work goes up and down, but our quarry's busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and ask Pete for more practice on the slope tips. I'd keep putting money aside, maybe 150 a month. Hannah and I might start looking at buying somewhere small in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If house building slows, the quarry cuts the agency drivers first, then the newest staff, which is me. It happened once before I started, I'm told. But we're busy now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and Hannah talk about when you talk about the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly a house and maybe a dog. She wants to stay at the primary school, and I'd like to drive a bigger truck one day. Nothing fancy.

say: I'd say **nothing much** changed, about what I expected.
We'd joke that the **weighbridge** is the only robot at the quarry.
think: I keep my job and get **better at tipping**.
Building work goes up and down, but our **quarry is busy**.
do: Ask the foreman for more **slope tipping** practice.
Start looking at **buying a home** with Hannah in a couple of years.
S0.quote: The weighbridge already prints my ticket without anyone touching it, and nobody at the quarry lost a job over that.
fieldNote: David uses the **weighbridge** as proof that automation can be harmless.
He knows newest staff go first in a **building slowdown**, but doesn't dwell on it.
His plans are **modest**: a house, a dog, a bigger truck.

steps.text: Ask the foreman for extra practice tipping on slopes
Save 150 a month towards a small home with Hannah

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big deal for office jobs, less so for us. I'd tell the lads to learn the new booking system when it comes in. Online, I'd keep out of arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is my hands on the wheel and my eyes on a muddy haul road, and no planning software changes that. The sales office and the dispatcher will probably shrink, and the booking will be done by software. That's not nice for them, but it's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new dispatch app once the other drivers had it sorted, probably asking Gaz, who's good with phones. I'd keep saving. And I'd ask the quarry whether they'd put me on the bigger articulated tipper course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sorry for the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Hannah's job at the school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says AI might do some of the marking and planning, but the kids still need someone to sit with them. I think she's safer than most. She worries more about pay than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not me. Is there anything in this picture that would make you nervous?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the dispatcher software started squeezing more trips out of us, then maybe. Faster means more risk on the haul road. But I'd see it coming.

say: I'd say this matters more for **office jobs** than drivers.
I'd tell the lads to learn the **booking system** when it arrives.
think: My day is mostly **hands on the wheel**, which planning software can't change.
The **sales office** and dispatcher would shrink, but not my job.
do: Learn the **dispatch app** once other drivers have it sorted.
Ask to go on the **articulated tipper** course.
feel: **Calm**, but a bit sorry for the office staff.
S1.quote: Most of my day is my hands on the wheel and my eyes on a muddy haul road, and no planning software changes that.
fieldNote: David clearly sees his job as **hands-on** and safe from thinking AI.
He trusts his partner's **school job** to hold up well.
His only worry is software **squeezing more trips**, a safety point.

steps.text: Learn the quarry's dispatch app with help from Gaz
Ask the quarry to fund the articulated tipper course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quarries will go first, and anyone who says otherwise hasn't seen the videos from the big mines. I'd say the government should make firms pay into a fund. At work I'd be quieter, because nobody wants to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quarries are private roads with no kids and no cyclists, so the self-driving tippers will start with drivers like me. I'd guess 2031, maybe even before. I'd be 32, and Hannah's wage alone wouldn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the quarry about training as a plant fitter, fixing the shovels and the crushers. I'd save harder, going from 150 to 300 a month, and we'd shelve the house. I'd also start looking at jobs on public roads, like council or bin lorries, as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground's moving under the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028, the robots three years later. What happens in those three years at the quarry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office goes, the weighbridge goes fully automatic, and someone starts mapping the haul roads for the robot trucks. I'd probably see the survey drones out there and know exactly what they're for. That's the worst bit, watching it being built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house, then the holiday we'd planned. Hannah and I would sit down and do a proper budget. I'd probably use one of those AI apps to do it, which is a bit funny.

say: I'd say **quarries go first**, as the big mines already show.
I'd say firms should pay into a **government fund**, but stay quiet at work.
think: Private quarry roads make **self-driving tippers** easy, so drivers like me go first.
At **32**, Hannah's wage alone wouldn't cover our rent.
do: Ask the quarry about training as a **plant fitter**.
Raise saving to **300 a month** and shelve the house.
Look at **council lorry jobs** on public roads as a backup.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the ground is moving under the truck.
S2.quote: Quarries are private roads with no kids and no cyclists, so the self-driving tippers will start with drivers like me.
fieldNote: David's calm flips because **quarries** are the easiest place for robot trucks.
He dreads **watching it being built**: drones mapping the haul roads.
He picks a **fitter** role and public-road driving as twin backups.

steps.text: Apply to train as a plant fitter at the quarry
Raise savings to 300 a month and shelve the house
Apply for council lorry jobs on public roads as a backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if the companies are honest with us. I'd ask the quarry managers straight out what their plan is. Online, maybe I'd share a couple of things about retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the quarry offered me a fitter's apprenticeship tomorrow, I'd take the pay cut and thank them. Robots around 2034 gives me a bit of time, but quarries will still be early. I'd want to be on the fixing side by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about the fitter apprenticeship in the first year and take it if they offered. If not, I'd do an evening course in heavy plant maintenance at the college. Hannah and I would still buy a small place, but only if one wage could cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels like I've got hold of the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A pay cut means less money. How would that work at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah's said she'd do more hours at the school if we needed it. We'd drive one car and stop eating out. It'd be tight for two or three years, but worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots need fewer fitters than you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be in the same boat as everyone, just with a better skill. I'm not certain, nobody is. But a fitter knows the machines, and that has to count for something.

say: I'd say five years is enough if **companies are honest**.
I'd ask quarry managers straight out about their **plan** for drivers.
think: I'd take a **fitter's apprenticeship** with a pay cut and be grateful.
Quarries will still be **early** even with robots arriving around 2034.
do: Ask about the **fitter apprenticeship** in year one and take it.
Otherwise take an evening course in **plant maintenance**.
Buy a small home only if **one wage** covers it.
feel: **Anxious**, but feeling I have hold of the wheel.
S3.quote: If the quarry offered me a fitter's apprenticeship tomorrow, I'd take the pay cut and thank them.
fieldNote: David trades **pay for security**, with his partner offering more hours.
He's honest that fitters may also be **needed less**.
The **one-wage** test now guides all big money decisions.

steps.text: Apply for the quarry's fitter apprenticeship in year one
Take an evening plant maintenance course if no apprenticeship comes
Buy a small home only if one wage covers the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to sort out a fair change, so let's do it properly. I'd tell younger lads at the quarry to learn a fixing trade. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd rather be the man who fixes the robot tipper than the man it replaced. Robots around 2039 means I'd be 40, with a trade by then. I think I'd be okay, honestly, if I start in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay driving for two or three years, then move into the fitter apprenticeship. I'd use AI tools more, for learning the manuals and diagnosing faults. Hannah and I would buy the house and maybe start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More of a plan than a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the plan go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quarry closing, or selling to a big company that brings its own fitters. Then I'd be looking for work with a half-finished trade. I'd try another quarry or a plant hire firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI more. You don't use it much now. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it actually work. Gaz showed me an app that reads the fault codes on the loader, and it was spot on. When I see it working, I'm in.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** to make a fair change.
I'd tell younger lads to learn a **fixing trade**, calmly.
think: I'd rather **fix the robot** tipper than be replaced by it.
By **40** I'd have a trade if I start in the next few years.
do: Drive two or three more years, then start the **fitter apprenticeship**.
Use **AI tools** to learn manuals and diagnose faults.
Buy the house and maybe **start a family** with Hannah.
feel: **Uneasy**, with more of a plan than a worry.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd rather be the man who fixes the robot tipper than the man it replaced.
fieldNote: A decade lets David's **steady** style work: watch, then move.
His risk is the quarry being **sold** to a bigger firm.
He adopts AI when he sees it work **in front of him**.

steps.text: Start the quarry fitter apprenticeship after two or three years
Use fault-code apps to learn loader and crusher repairs
Buy a house with Hannah and plan a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because quarries would get robot trucks first and I'd have no trade by 2031. What would help is the quarry offering apprenticeships early, and some kind of fund that tops up pay while drivers retrain. My partner Hannah earns less than me but her job will outlast mine, and we've started joking about who'll be staying at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but a robot tipper on a slope next to a man with a shovel worries me. Someone needs to check those things properly.

headlineQuote: My partner Hannah earns less than me but her job will outlast mine, and we've started joking about who'll be staying at home.
portrait: David Young, 27, drives a **quarry tipper** and is still learning to tip on slopes.
He's calm when AI stalls or stays in offices, trusting his **hands-on** work.
In the fast picture he expects **quarries** to get robot trucks first and moves towards plant fitting.
With more time he plans a **fitter apprenticeship**, a house and maybe a family with Hannah.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because quarries would automate first and he'd have no trade by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Early **apprenticeships** at the quarry and a fund that tops up pay during retraining.
